meta.title: Python Programming Language
meta.subtitle: From zero to a PyRaylib game — the second scripting language embedded in GnuchanOS.

sections.title: Why Python?
paragraphs: Python is the second language GnuchanOS embeds, next to Lua. Where Lua aims to be small and fast, Python aims to be readable: indentation replaces braces, and the standard library is enormous. The GCL runtime starts a CPython interpreter through the Embed module and hands it a raylib window, so a Python script can open a window, draw and play sound with no build step.
The Python track has two halves, exactly like the Lua track. The first half teaches the language. The second half teaches PyRaylib and PyRaygui, the bindings that expose raylib and raygui to Python.

notes.text: Everything here runs on the Python that ships with GnuchanOS (Library/Embeded/Python_Runtime/Python.dll) together with PyRaylib.dll, PyRaygui.dll and the helper module gcl.

sections.title: Your First Program
paragraphs: print is a function, not a statement. It accepts any number of values and separates them with a single space.

code.src:
print("Hello from Python!")
print("One line", "and another value")

sections.output:
Hello from Python!
One line and another value

sections.title: Indentation Is Syntax
paragraphs: Python has no braces and no end. A block is marked by indenting it. The convention is four spaces, and the only real rule is that a block must be indented consistently.
Mixing tabs and spaces in the same block is a syntax error. Most editors, including the GnuchanOS IDE, insert four spaces when you press Tab inside a .py file.

code.src:
score = 7

if score > 5:
    print("good")
    print("really good")   # still inside the if

print("done")             # back outside

sections.title: Comments
paragraphs: A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line.
Python has no block comment. A triple-quoted string standing on its own is not a comment, but it is ignored when nothing is assigned to it, so it is the usual way to park a paragraph of explanation.

code.src:
# a full line comment

x = 5  # a trailing comment

"""
A triple-quoted string standing on its own
is ignored by the interpreter.
"""

print(x)

sections.title: Three Ways to Run Python
paragraphs: The interpreter is always the same; only the entry point changes.
1. Standalone file. The GCL CLI can run a Python file directly.
2. From GCL. The Embed module starts a Python process and can share variables with it.
3. From the IDE. A project created with the Python switch on already contains scripts/main.py.

code.src:
# 1. run a file directly
gcl -pyrun hello.py

# 2. start Python from a GCL program
#    (main.gcsf)
#    #native <Embed>
#    Embed.Run(type="python");
#    Embed.Stop(type="python");

# 3. build a project that opens a Python window
gcl -build project.gcdata

notes.text: When Python runs under GCL, the modules raylib, raygui and gcl are already importable. You still write the import line, but you never install anything: the runtime resolves them next to the interpreter.
Only one Python process at a time. Embed.Run(type="python") twice starts nothing the second time. Python and Lua together is fine.

sections.title: Names Are Labels
paragraphs: Python is dynamically typed: a variable is a name bound to a value, and the value carries the type. Assigning a different type to the same name is fine.
type() tells you what you are holding.

code.src:
x = 10
print(type(x))

x = "now a string"
print(type(x))

count = 3
count = count + 1
print(count)

sections.title: The Core Types
paragraphs: Six types cover almost everything you write before reaching for a library.

sections.title: Numbers
paragraphs: There are two number types to care about: int and float. Integers have no size limit, so 2 ** 100 is exact.
/ always produces a float. // is integer division and rounds toward negative infinity. % is the remainder, and ** is the power operator.

code.src:
a = 7
b = 2

print(a / b)     # true division
print(a // b)    # floor division
print(a % b)     # remainder
print(a ** b)    # power
print(2 ** 100)

f = 0.1 + 0.2
print(f)
print(round(f, 2))

sections.title: Truth and None
paragraphs: True and False are capitalised. Almost every value has a truth value: zero, empty text, empty collections and None are falsey, everything else is truthy. You almost never need to compare against True explicitly.
None is a real value meaning "nothing here". A function that returns nothing returns None. Test it with is None, never with == None.

code.src:
print(bool(0), bool(1))
print(bool(""), bool("x"))
print(bool([]), bool([1]))

result = None
if result is None:
    print("nothing came back")

name = ""
print("anonymous" if not name else name)

sections.output:
False True
False True
False True
nothing came back
anonymous

sections.title: Text and f-strings
paragraphs: Strings are immutable: every string operation produces a new string. Single and double quotes are equivalent; a backslash escapes.

An f-string is a string prefixed with f in which { } is replaced by the value of the expression inside it. This is the normal way to build output; it replaces both concatenation and C-style placeholders.

code.src:
name = "GnuChan"
score = 42
ratio = 0.5

print(f"{name} has {score} points")
print(f"ratio as percent: {ratio:.0%}")
print(f"padded: {score:5d}|{name:>10}|")
print("a" + "b", "x" * 3)
print(len(name))

sections.output:
GnuChan has 42 points
ratio as percent: 50%
padded:    42|   GnuChan|
ab xxx
7

sections.title: Arithmetic and Comparison
paragraphs: The arithmetic operators are + - * / // % ** and the augmented forms += -= *= /= //= %= **=.
Comparison uses == != < <= > >=. You can chain them the way maths writes them: 0 < x < 10 is one expression and means exactly what it says.

sections.title: Logic
paragraphs: The boolean operators are the words and, or and not — there is no && or ||.
and and or do not return booleans: they return one of their operands. That makes or the standard default-value idiom.

code.src:
print(True and False)
print(True or False)
print(not False)

# 'or' returns the first truthy operand
speed = None
speed = speed or 5
print(speed)

# short circuit: the right side never runs
name = ""
print(name and name.upper())

sections.title: Membership and Identity
paragraphs: in asks whether a value is inside a collection or a string. not in is its negation.
is asks whether two names point at the same object. It is not the same question as ==, which asks whether two values are equal. Use is only for None and for booleans.

code.src:
print(2 in [1, 2, 3])
print('ell' in 'hello')
print(9 not in [1, 2, 3])

empty = []
print(empty is None)
print(empty == [])

copy = list(empty)
print(copy is empty)

sections.output:
True
True
True
False
True
False

sections.title: Conditional Expressions
paragraphs: A conditional expression is a one-line if: a if condition else b. It is an expression, so it can sit on the right of an assignment or inside an f-string.

code.src:
score = 71
grade = "pass" if score >= 50 else "fail"
print(grade)

lives = 0
print(f"{lives} lives left" if lives else "game over")

sections.title: if, elif, else
paragraphs: A condition is followed by a colon; the body is the indented block. There is no else if — the keyword is elif. The chain is checked top to bottom and the first true branch wins.
The condition needs no parentheses. Parentheses are only ever grouping in Python, never part of the syntax.

sections.title: while
paragraphs: while repeats as long as its condition is true. A while True: with a break inside is the usual shape of a game loop.

code.src:
count = 0

while count < 5:
    count += 1
    print(f"tick {count}")

print(f"stopped at {count}")

sections.output:
tick 1
tick 2
tick 3
tick 4
tick 5
stopped at 5

sections.title: for and range
paragraphs: A Python for is a for-each: it walks the items of a sequence. There is no counter to declare and no condition to write.
range(n) produces the numbers 0 to n-1. It is lazy: nothing is stored. The three forms are range(stop), range(start, stop) and range(start, stop, step).
sections.output:
hello Ada
hello Grace
hello Alan
0 1 2 
10 7 4 1 
5050

sections.title: break, continue, and the for-else
paragraphs: break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips to the next iteration.
A for may carry an else block. It runs when the loop finishes without hitting a break. It reads oddly at first and is genuinely useful for "searched everything and found nothing".

sections.title: Iterating with Index
paragraphs: enumerate() gives you the position and the value together, which removes the need for range(len(items)).
zip() walks several sequences in parallel and stops at the shortest.

code.src:
highscores = [120, 340, 90]

for i, value in enumerate(highscores):
    print(f"#{i + 1}: {value}")

names = ["Ada", "Grace"]
scores = [120, 340]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name} = {score}")

sections.title: Defining a Function
paragraphs: def introduces a function. The body is the indented block. There is no return type to write, and a function may be defined after the code that calls it as long as the call itself happens later.

code.src:
def greet(name):
    print(f"hello {name}")

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

greet("GnuChan")
print(add(2, 3))
print(add("a", "b"))   # + is overloaded for text

sections.title: Return Values
paragraphs: A function with no return, or a bare return, gives back None.
A return with several comma-separated values packs them into a tuple. The caller can unpack it straight into several names — this is the normal way to hand back more than one value.

sections.title: Default and Keyword Arguments
paragraphs: A parameter may declare a default. Arguments may then be passed by position or by name; naming them makes a call read like a sentence and lets you skip the ones in between.
Never use a mutable object such as a list as a default — it is created once and shared by every call. Use None and build the value inside.

code.src:
def window(width, height, title="Untitled", fps=60):
    print(f"{title}: {width}x{height} at {fps} fps")

window(800, 600)
window(800, 600, "Game")
window(height=600, width=800, fps=30)

def append_to(item, target=None):
    if target is None:
        target = []
    target.append(item)
    return target

print(append_to(1))
print(append_to(2))

sections.output:
Untitled: 800x600 at 60 fps
Game: 800x600 at 60 fps
Untitled: 800x600 at 30 fps
[1]
[2]

sections.title: Variadic Arguments
paragraphs: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. The two names are a convention, not a requirement — the stars are what matter.
A star also spreads a sequence at the call site.

sections.title: Scope
paragraphs: A name assigned inside a function is local to that function. Reading an outer name works; assigning to it does not, unless you declare global (module level) or nonlocal (the enclosing function).

code.src:
counter = 0

def bump():
    global counter
    counter += 1

def peek():
    return counter          # reading the outer name is fine

def shadow():
    counter = 99           # a new local, the outer one is untouched
    return counter

bump()
bump()
print(peek())
print(shadow())
print(counter)

sections.title: Lambdas
paragraphs: A lambda is a function expression: parameters, then a colon, then a single expression that is returned. It has no body block and no statement inside it.
Its real home is a short callback passed to another function.

code.src:
square = lambda n: n * n
print(square(6))

scores = [("Ada", 120), ("Grace", 340), ("Alan", 90)]
scores.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
for name, score in scores:
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

sections.title: Lists
paragraphs: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence written with square brackets. Indexing starts at 0, and a negative index counts from the end: -1 is the last item.
A slice start:stop takes a copy of a range, excluding the stop index. Leaving a side empty means "from the beginning" or "to the end".
The methods you will use constantly are append, insert, remove, pop, sort and the built-ins len, sum, min, max, sorted.

code.src:
numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]

print(numbers[0], numbers[-1])
print(numbers[1:3])

numbers.append(9)
numbers[0] = 100
print(numbers)
print(len(numbers), sum(numbers), max(numbers))

numbers.remove(1)
print(numbers)
print(sorted(numbers))

sections.title: Tuples
paragraphs: A tuple is an ordered sequence that cannot be changed after it is built. It is written with parentheses, and it is the type a function returns when it hands back several values at once.
Unpacking is the reason tuples are everywhere: x, y = point assigns both names in one line.
A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma — (5,) is a tuple, (5) is just the number 5.

code.src:
point = (10, 20)

x, y = point
print(x, y)
print(point[1])

single = (5,)
print(type(single), single)

not_a_tuple = (5)
print(type(not_a_tuple))

sections.title: Dictionaries
paragraphs: A dictionary maps keys to values, written { key: value }. Lookup is by key and is fast, which makes a dict the natural choice for a lookup table or a small record.
Reading a missing key with d[key] raises KeyError. d.get(key, default) returns the default instead, and in tests for a key without raising.
Iterating a dict walks its keys. .items() walks key and value together, .keys() and .values() walk one side.

code.src:
player = {"name": "Ada", "score": 120}

print(player["name"])

player["score"] = 200
player["level"] = 3
print(player.get("missing", 0))

for key, value in player.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

print("name" in player)
print(sorted(player.keys()))

sections.output:
Ada
0
name: Ada
score: 200
level: 3
True
['level', 'name', 'score']

sections.title: Sets
paragraphs: A set holds unique values with no order. It is written with braces, and the set operators are the ones from maths: | union, & intersection, - difference, ^ symmetric difference.
Because a set is unordered, never print one and expect a particular sequence. Sort it first when the order matters.

code.src:
a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {3, 4}

print(sorted(a | b))
print(sorted(a & b))
print(sorted(a - b))

a.add(9)
print(9 in a)
print(len(a))

print(len({1, 1, 2, 2, 3}))

sections.title: Names, References, and Copies
paragraphs: Assigning a list to a second name does not copy it — both names point at the same list, and changing it through one name is visible through the other.
To get an independent list, take a full slice a[:], call list(a), or use a.copy(). Tuples and strings are immutable, so this never arises with them.

code.src:
a = [1, 2]
b = a            # the same list under another name
b.append(3)
print(a)

c = a[:]         # an independent copy
c.append(9)
print(a)
print(c)

sections.title: Indexing and Slicing
paragraphs: A string is a sequence of characters, so everything you learned about list indexing applies: [i], negative indexes, and slices.
A slice with a step of -1 reverses the text. Nothing is modified in place — every operation returns a new string.

code.src:
text = "GnuchanOS"

print(text[0], text[-1])
print(text[0:4])
print(text[4:])
print(text[::-1])
print("chan" in text)
print(len(text))

sections.output:
G S
Gnuc
hanOS
SOnahcunG
True
9

sections.title: The Common Methods
paragraphs: Strings carry a large method set; these are the ones a game or a tool actually uses.

rows: Cut into a list of parts
Glue a list into one string

code.src:
raw = "  Hello World  "

print(repr(raw.strip()))
print(raw.lower())
print(raw.upper())
print("a,b,c".split(","))
print("-".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
print("hello".replace("l", "L"))
print("abc".startswith("ab"), "abc".endswith("z"))
print("banana".count("an"))

sections.output:
'Hello World'
  hello world  
  HELLO WORLD  
['a', 'b', 'c']
a-b-c
heLLo
True False
2

sections.title: Converting Between Text and Numbers
paragraphs: int() and float() parse text, and str() renders a value. Input that arrives from a file, a command line or a dialog is always text first.
An f-string can also format a number: {value:x} is hexadecimal, {value:b} is binary, {value:.3f} fixes three decimals.

sections.title: Escapes and Raw Strings
paragraphs: Inside a normal string, a backslash introduces an escape: \n, \t, \\, \".
A raw string is prefixed with r and does not process escapes. This is what you want for Windows paths, where \t in C:\temp would otherwise become a tab.
A triple-quoted string may span several lines without any escape at all.

code.src:
print("line one\nline two")
print("col1\tcol2")

path = r"C:\Games\my project"
print(path)

text = """first
second
third"""
print(text.count("\n") + 1)

sections.output:
line one
line two
col1	col2
C:\Games\my project
3

sections.title: import
paragraphs: A module is a file of Python code. import name makes it available under that name; from name import thing pulls one member into the current namespace; import name as alias renames it.

Imports belong at the top of the file. The interpreter finds the module on its search path, which the embedded runtime has already extended with the directory of your script and the runtime library directory — that is why import raylib works with nothing installed.

code.src:
import math
from math import sqrt
import random as rng

print(math.pi)
print(sqrt(16))
print(rng.randint(1, 6) >= 1)

sections.title: math and random
paragraphs: math works in radians, unlike the Math module in GCL which takes degrees. pi and e are constants on the module.
random produces pseudo-random numbers. Call random.seed(n) when you want a run to be reproducible — for a game you usually do not.

rows: Round down / up to an integer
An int from a to b inclusive

code.src:
import math
import random

print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2))
print(round(math.sin(0), 3))

random.seed(7)
roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print(1 <= roll <= 6)
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]) in ["rock", "paper", "scissors"])

sections.title: os, time and json
paragraphs: os.path builds and splits paths correctly for the operating system you are on. This matters more than it looks: joining strings with a slash works on one platform and not the other.
time gives you a monotonic clock, which is what a delta-time loop should use. json turns dictionaries into text and back, which is the simplest way to save a settings file or a highscore table.

code.src:
import os
import json
import time

print(os.path.join("assets", "icon.png"))
print(os.path.splitext("game.py"))

start = time.time()
time.sleep(0.01)
print(time.time() - start >= 0.01)

data = {"name": "Ada", "score": 120}
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(text)
print(json.loads(text) == data)

sections.title: Reading and Writing Files
paragraphs: open(path, mode) gives you a file object. The modes are "r" read (the default), "w" write and truncate, and "a" append.

Always open a file inside a with block. The block closes the file when it ends, even if an exception is raised inside it — without with you would have to call close() yourself and remember to do it on every path out.
Iterating a file yields one line at a time, each ending with a newline, so strip it before parsing.

code.src:
with open("scores.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Ada 120\n")
    f.write("Grace 340\n")

total = 0
with open("scores.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.split()
        total += int(score)
        print(name, score)

print("total", total)

sections.title: Your Own Modules
paragraphs: Any .py file next to your script is importable by its file name without the extension. In a GnuchanOS project the scripts live in scripts/, and that directory is on the path, so scripts/player.py is imported as import player.
The one trap is the entry file itself. A file run directly is __main__, so guard anything that should only run when the file is the entry point with if __name__ == "__main__":.

sections.title: A Class
paragraphs: class defines a new type. The constructor is the method named __init__, and its first parameter is self — the instance being built. Every method takes self first; Python passes it for you, you never pass it yourself.
Attributes are created simply by assigning them: self.name = name. There is no declaration list.

code.src:
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name, score=0):
        self.name = name
        self.score = score

    def add(self, points):
        self.score += points
        return self.score

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name} ({self.score})"

p = Player("Ada")
p.add(10)
p.add(5)
print(p)
print(p.score)
print(p.name)

sections.title: Dunder Methods
paragraphs: Methods whose names begin and end with two underscores are called by the language itself, not by you. They are how a class plugs into operators, printing and built-ins.
__str__ decides what print shows. __len__ makes len() work. __eq__ decides what == means.

sections.title: Inheritance
paragraphs: A class may extend another by naming it in parentheses. The child inherits every method it does not replace, and super() calls the parent's version of a method you are overriding.
isinstance(obj, ClassName) is true for the class and for everything it inherits from.

sections.title: try and except
paragraphs: An error raises an exception. If nothing catches it the program stops and prints a traceback. try marks the code that might fail; except handles a particular kind of failure.
Catch the narrowest exception you can name. A bare except: swallows everything, including the typing mistake you were trying to find.

sections.title: finally, else and raise
paragraphs: finally runs whether or not an exception happened — it is where cleanup belongs. else runs only when no exception was raised, which keeps the try block to the single line that can fail.
raise throws an exception yourself. Raising with a message is how a function refuses input instead of returning a meaningless value.

sections.title: The Exceptions You Will Actually Meet
paragraphs: Each of these names a real mistake, and the name is the fastest way to find it.

rows: "a" + 1 — the operation does not apply to that type
A sequence index past the end
A dictionary lookup that does not exist
open() on a path that is not there
Calling a method the object does not have
Using a name that was never assigned

sections.title: Three Functions
paragraphs: When Python runs under GCL there is one extra module: gcl. It has exactly three members, and it is the whole bridge between the two languages.

rows: Connect to the shared state block

notes.text: Shared values are numbers. Text travels by convention: store a length and a code, not a string.

sections.title: How the State Is Shared
paragraphs: The state block is a small shared store that the GCL side also reaches through Embed.SendValue and Embed.GetValue. Both sides read and write the same named slots, so a Python script and a GCL program can exchange values without opening a socket or parsing a file.
Always call gcl.init() before the first get_state or set_state.

sections.title: The Python Side
paragraphs: The script reads with gcl.get_state and writes with gcl.set_state. Names must match on both sides — they are plain strings, so a typo reads None instead of raising an error.
That None is the one thing to guard. A slot that was never written comes back as None, and adding to it would raise TypeError. The idiom is value = gcl.get_state("x") or 0.0.

code.src:
import gcl

gcl.init()

target = gcl.get_state("target") or 0.0
speed = gcl.get_state("speed") or 1.0

x = 0.0
score = 0

while x < target:
    x += speed
    score += 1

# publish the result for the GCL side
gcl.set_state("score", score)
print(f"reached {x} in {score} steps")

sections.title: Two Processes, Two Windows
paragraphs: GCL can run Python and Lua at the same time — each is one process with its own window, and they talk through the same shared values. That is exactly how the Pong example in the GCL track works: Lua owns the left half of the world, Python owns the right half, and only the ball state is shared.
The demo lives in language/examples/demo_pong_lua_vs_python/; scripts/main.py there is a complete, runnable example of this chapter.

notes.text: Only one process per type: Embed.Run(type="python") twice starts nothing the second time. Python plus Lua together is fine.

sections.title: What PyRaylib Is
paragraphs: PyRaylib is a Python extension module that registers raylib's functions into a module called raylib. It is loaded for you: when GCL starts a Python script it adds the runtime directory to the search path and resolves raylib and raygui from there, so there is nothing to install and no build step.
The names are raylib's own names in CamelCase: InitWindow, DrawText, IsKeyDown. If you know the C API, you already know this binding.

sections.title: The Game Loop
paragraphs: Every raylib program has the same shape: open a window, loop until the user closes it, draw one frame per iteration, then close. In Python the loop is an ordinary while and the condition is the return value of WindowShouldClose, which the binding returns as a real bool.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "My First PyRaylib Window")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(50, 50, 200, 100, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawText("Hello from Python + raylib", 20, 20, 30, raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.DrawFPS(10, 10)

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Everything after InitWindow belongs inside the loop except CloseWindow. Drawing outside BeginDrawing / EndDrawing has no effect.

sections.title: Colors and Key Constants
paragraphs: A color is a single packed integer, not an object. Every raylib color is an attribute of the module: raylib.RED, raylib.DARKPURPLE, raylib.BLANK and so on. Functions that want a color simply take that integer, and nothing has to be converted.
Key and mouse constants have the same shape and the same integer type: raylib.KEY_SPACE, raylib.KEY_LEFT, raylib.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT.
The colors the binding publishes are listed below. Fade(color, alpha) and ColorAlpha(color, alpha) build a new color from an existing one, and Color(r, g, b, a) builds one from components.

code.src:
import raylib

print(type(raylib.RED).__name__)
print(raylib.RED > 0)
print(raylib.KEY_SPACE, raylib.KEY_ESCAPE)

faded = raylib.Fade(raylib.RED, 0.5)
print(faded != raylib.RED)

sections.title: Shapes
paragraphs: Every shape function takes plain numbers and an integer color. Coordinates are in pixels with the origin at the top-left of the window, and y grows downwards.
The functions whose C version takes a Vector2 have been flattened here: DrawCircleV in C becomes the same call as DrawCircle, taking x, y as two numbers rather than a vector.

rows: DrawRectangleRounded(x, y, w, h, roundness, segments, color)
DrawTriangle(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, color)

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(640, 360, "Shapes")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(20, 20, 120, 80, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawRectangleLines(20, 120, 120, 80, raylib.DARKBLUE)
    raylib.DrawRectangleRounded(20, 220, 120, 80, 0.4, 8, raylib.GREEN)

    raylib.DrawCircle(220, 60, 40, raylib.BLUE)
    raylib.DrawCircleLines(220, 160, 40, raylib.DARKGREEN)

    raylib.DrawLine(160, 300, 320, 240, raylib.MAROON)
    raylib.DrawLineEx(340, 300, 500, 240, 3.0, raylib.PURPLE)

    raylib.DrawTriangle(520, 300, 560, 140, 620, 300, raylib.ORANGE)

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Shape functions take integers for positions and a float for a radius or a thickness. Python will not convert for you, so an expression that produces a float position needs int(round(...)).

sections.title: Text
paragraphs: DrawText uses raylib's built-in font and is all you need for a debug readout or a prototype.

A loaded font is returned as a two-element tuple: the base size and the texture id. DrawTextEx expects exactly those two values first, so the clean way to call it is with a star-unpack — raylib.DrawTextEx(*font, text, ...) — which is also self-documenting about what the tuple holds.

rows: DrawTextEx(baseSize, id, text, x, y, size, spacing, color)
Load a TTF at a pixel size
Load a TTF at its natural size
The built-in font as a tuple

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(640, 200, "Text")

font = raylib.LoadFontEx("assets/FreeMono.ttf", 32)
print("font tuple has", len(font), "entries")
print("measured:", raylib.MeasureText("hello", 20))

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.DrawText("default font", 20, 20, 20, raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.DrawTextEx(*font, "custom font", 20, 60, 32, 2, raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.DrawText("centred-ish", 20, 120, 20, raylib.MAROON)

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.UnloadFont(*font)
raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Textures
paragraphs: LoadTexture returns an integer handle for the texture on the GPU, and you pass that handle to every draw and finally to UnloadTexture.
DrawTexture places it at a position with a tint; DrawTextureEx adds rotation and scale. Pass raylib.WHITE as the tint when you want the image unchanged.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(640, 360, "Textures")

logo = raylib.LoadTexture("assets/logo.png")
print("texture valid:", raylib.IsTextureValid(logo))

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)

    raylib.DrawTexture(logo, 20, 20, raylib.WHITE)
    raylib.DrawTextureEx(logo, 220, 20, 45.0, 0.5, raylib.WHITE)

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.UnloadTexture(logo)
raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Rectangles Are Tuples
paragraphs: raylib.Rectangle(x, y, w, h) builds a tuple. That is what the raygui binding expects as its first argument, and it is what makes a layout easy to express once and reuse.
The raylib shape functions want the four numbers separately, so spread the tuple with a star when you want to draw it: raylib.DrawRectangleRec(*box, color).

code.src:
import raylib

box = raylib.Rectangle(40, 40, 200, 100)
print(box, type(box).__name__)

x, y, w, h = box
print(x, y, w, h)

raylib.InitWindow(320, 200, "Rectangle")
raylib.BeginDrawing()
raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)
raylib.DrawRectangleRec(*box, raylib.SKYBLUE)
raylib.EndDrawing()
raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Keyboard
paragraphs: There are two questions you can ask about a key, and the difference matters. IsKeyDown is true for every frame the key is held — that is what movement uses. IsKeyPressed is true for exactly one frame, the frame the key went down — that is what a menu or a fire action uses.
Because both return a real bool, they read naturally in an if.

rows: The key went down this frame
The key came up this frame
Key code of the next key in the queue, 0 if none
Unicode codepoint of the next typed character

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(640, 360, "Keyboard")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

x, y = 300.0, 160.0
speed = 200.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    dt = raylib.GetFrameTime()

    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_LEFT):
        x -= speed * dt
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_RIGHT):
        x += speed * dt
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_UP):
        y -= speed * dt
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_DOWN):
        y += speed * dt

    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_SPACE):
        x, y = 300.0, 160.0

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.DrawRectangle(int(x), int(y), 40, 40, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawText("arrows move, space resets", 20, 20, 20, raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Multiplying by GetFrameTime() makes movement independent of the frame rate. Without it the paddle moves twice as fast on a machine drawing twice as many frames.

sections.title: Mouse
paragraphs: GetMouseX and GetMouseY give the position as two integers. GetMousePosition gives the same pair as a tuple, which unpacks on assignment: mx, my = raylib.GetMousePosition().
GetMouseWheelMove returns a float that is positive when scrolled up, and the button tests mirror the keyboard ones.

rows: The same as a (x, y) tuple

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(640, 360, "Mouse")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

radius = 20.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    mx, my = raylib.GetMousePosition()
    radius += raylib.GetMouseWheelMove() * 2
    radius = max(4.0, min(120.0, radius))

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)

    if raylib.IsMouseButtonDown(raylib.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT):
        raylib.DrawCircle(int(mx), int(my), radius, raylib.RED)
    else:
        raylib.DrawCircleLines(int(mx), int(my), radius, raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.DrawText(f"{int(mx)}, {int(my)}", 10, 10, 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Text Input
paragraphs: GetCharPressed returns one typed character at a time as a codepoint, and 0 when the queue is empty. Loop until it returns 0 to drain everything typed in that frame.
For a text field the usual pair is GetCharPressed for the characters and IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_BACKSPACE) for the delete key.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(480, 160, "Typing")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

text = ""

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    while True:
        code = raylib.GetCharPressed()
        if code == 0:
            break
        if 32 <= code < 127:
            text += chr(code)

    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_BACKSPACE) and text:
        text = text[:-1]

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.DrawRectangleLines(20, 20, 440, 40, raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.DrawText(text, 30, 30, 20, raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Camera2D Is a Dictionary
paragraphs: The Python binding does not expose C structs as opaque objects. raylib.Camera2D() returns a dictionary with four keys — offset, target, rotation and zoom — where offset and target are themselves dictionaries holding x and y.
That is convenient: you read and write the camera like any other dict, and BeginMode2D(cam) reads it fresh every frame. Everything you draw between BeginMode2D and EndMode2D is transformed by it.
target is the world point that appears at offset on screen. With a zero offset and a target at the middle of the map, the camera sits exactly there.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "Camera2D")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

cam = raylib.Camera2D()
cam["offset"] = {"x": 400.0, "y": 300.0}
cam["target"] = {"x": 400.0, "y": 300.0}
cam["zoom"] = 1.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    cam["zoom"] += raylib.GetMouseWheelMove() * 0.1
    cam["zoom"] = max(0.2, min(4.0, cam["zoom"]))

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.BeginMode2D(cam)
    for i in range(0, 9):
        raylib.DrawRectangle(100 + i * 80, 250, 60, 100, raylib.SKYBLUE)
    raylib.EndMode2D()

    raylib.DrawText(f"zoom {cam['zoom']:.2f}", 20, 20, 20, raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: To find out what a mouse position means in the world, pass the camera to GetScreenToWorld2D; the reverse is GetWorldToScreen2D. Both take the camera dictionary.

sections.title: Camera3D
paragraphs: raylib.Camera3D() returns a dictionary with position, target and up — each a dictionary with x, y, z — plus fovy and projection. Set the fields you care about and pass the whole dictionary to BeginMode3D.
projection selects perspective or orthographic with the constants raylib.CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE and raylib.CAMERA_ORTHOGRAPHIC.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "Camera3D")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

cam = raylib.Camera3D()
cam["position"] = {"x": 10.0, "y": 10.0, "z": 10.0}
cam["target"] = {"x": 0.0, "y": 0.0, "z": 0.0}
print(cam["projection"] == raylib.CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.BeginMode3D(cam)
    raylib.DrawCube(0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawCubeWires(0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2, raylib.MAROON)
    raylib.DrawGrid(10, 1.0)
    raylib.EndMode3D()

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Shapes in 3D
paragraphs: The 3D shape functions are flattened the same way as the 2D ones: a Vector3 becomes three separate float arguments.

rows: DrawCube(x, y, z, w, h, l, color)
DrawCubeWires(x, y, z, w, h, l, color)
DrawCylinder(x, y, z, rTop, rBottom, height, sides, color)
DrawLine3D(x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, color)

code.src:
raylib.DrawSphere(-4, 1, 0, 1.0, raylib.BLUE)
raylib.DrawCylinder(0, 1, 0, 0.5, 0.5, 2.0, 16, raylib.GREEN)
raylib.DrawPlane(0, 0, 0, 20, 20, raylib.LIGHTGRAY)

sections.title: Opening the Device
paragraphs: Audio is started explicitly with InitAudioDevice() and released with CloseAudioDevice(). Between the two, IsAudioDeviceReady() reports whether a device actually opened — worth checking, because a machine without a sound device would otherwise fail later with a confusing error.

rows: Short effect, whole file in memory

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Audio")
raylib.InitAudioDevice()

print("device ready:", raylib.IsAudioDeviceReady())
raylib.SetMasterVolume(0.5)
print("volume:", raylib.GetMasterVolume())

raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Sound and Music Handles
paragraphs: LoadSound and LoadMusicStream return an integer handle, exactly like a texture. Store it in a variable and pass it to PlaySound or UpdateMusicStream.

Trigger a sound from inside an input check so it fires once per event rather than once per frame. Feed a music stream with UpdateMusicStream on every frame or it plays for a fraction of a second and stops.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Sound")
raylib.InitAudioDevice()

beep = raylib.LoadSound("assets/beep.wav")
raylib.SetMasterVolume(0.5)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_SPACE):
        raylib.PlaySound(beep)

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.DrawText("press space to beep", 40, 90, 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.UnloadSound(beep)
raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: The sound and music handles in this binding are still being finished: the value returned by LoadSound is derived from the audio stream rather than being a unique handle, so PlaySound may not play the file you loaded. Treat the device calls and SetMasterVolume as stable today, and check IsAudioDeviceReady() before relying on playback.

sections.title: Music Streams
paragraphs: Music is streamed from disk so a track can be minutes long — but the stream must be fed every frame with UpdateMusicStream(m). Forget that call and the music plays for a fraction of a second and stops.
Put it at the top of the loop, next to the input checks.

code.src:
import raylib

raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Music")
raylib.InitAudioDevice()

music = raylib.LoadMusicStream("assets/theme.ogg")
raylib.PlayMusicStream(music)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.UpdateMusicStream(music)     # must run every frame

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.DrawText("playing", 150, 90, 24, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Every loaded sound and music stream is memory. Free them with UnloadSound / UnloadMusicStream when the game ends.

sections.title: The Rectangle Comes First
paragraphs: The raygui binding is rect-first: a widget takes a rectangle as its first argument and the label after it. The rectangle is the tuple produced by raylib.Rectangle(x, y, w, h), so the same tuple can be reused for a widget, a hit test and a layout that you draw yourself.

Widgets return their new state: a button returns a bool, a slider returns a number, a combo box returns the selected index. Nothing is stored inside the widget — you keep the value and pass it back in every frame.

code.src:
import raylib
import raygui

raylib.InitWindow(600, 400, "raygui")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

button = raylib.Rectangle(20, 20, 200, 40)
slider = raylib.Rectangle(20, 80, 300, 30)
check  = raylib.Rectangle(20, 130, 24, 24)

width = 200.0
fullscreen = False

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    if raygui.GuiButton(button, "Reset"):
        width = 200.0

    width = raygui.GuiSlider(slider, "", "Width", width, 50.0, 500.0)
    fullscreen = raygui.GuiCheckBox(check, "Fullscreen", fullscreen)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(20, 180, int(width), 60, raylib.SKYBLUE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: A widget draws and answers in the same call, so it belongs inside the frame. The rectangle is in screen pixels, not world pixels — draw widgets after EndMode2D so the camera does not move them.

sections.title: The Widget Set
paragraphs: The signatures below are the ones to memorise. Every one takes the rectangle first.

code.src:
import raylib
import raygui

raylib.InitWindow(560, 420, "Settings")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

panel   = raylib.Rectangle(20, 20, 520, 380)
vol     = raylib.Rectangle(40, 90, 460, 28)
prog    = raylib.Rectangle(40, 140, 460, 24)
quality = raylib.Rectangle(40, 190, 220, 28)
close   = raylib.Rectangle(180, 330, 200, 40)

volume = 0.7
quality_index = 1

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raygui.GuiPanel(panel, "Settings")
    raygui.GuiLabel(raylib.Rectangle(40, 60, 200, 20), "Audio")

    volume = raygui.GuiSlider(vol, "Vol", "", volume, 0.0, 1.0)
    raygui.GuiProgressBar(prog, "", f"{volume:.0%}", volume, 0.0, 1.0)
    quality_index = raygui.GuiComboBox(quality, "Low;Normal;High", quality_index)

    if raygui.GuiButton(close, "Close"):
        break

    raylib.DrawText(f"quality index {quality_index}", 40, 240, 20, raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Styling
paragraphs: GuiSetStyle(control, property, value) changes a widget's colours, sizes and padding, and GuiGetStyle(control, property) reads one back. GuiLoadStyle(path) loads a raygui style file in one call, and GuiLoadStyleDefault() restores the built-in look.

One caveat to know before you reach for it: the Python binding does not export the GuiControl and GuiControlProperty constant tables, so those two arguments have to be written as plain numbers (they are documented in raygui's own header).

rows: Enable or grey out all widgets

code.src:
import raygui

before = raygui.GuiGetStyle(0, 16)
raygui.GuiSetStyle(0, 16, 20)
after = raygui.GuiGetStyle(0, 16)
print(before, after)

raygui.GuiLoadStyleDefault()
print(raygui.GuiGetTextWidth("MMMMMMMMMM") > 0)

sections.title: What We Are Building
paragraphs: One window, one paddle, one ball, a score, and a restart button. It uses every part of this track: dictionaries and functions for state, a class-free module layout, input, drawing, and a raygui button.
The shape of the file is the shape of every game you will write: constants → state → update → draw → loop.

code.src:
import raylib
import raygui
import gcl

gcl.init()

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H = 120, 16
BALL_R = 8
PADDLE_SPEED = 420.0
BALL_SPEED_X = 200.0
BALL_SPEED_Y = 260.0

raylib.InitWindow(WIDTH, HEIGHT, "Keep-Up")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

paddle_x = WIDTH / 2 - PADDLE_W / 2
ball_x, ball_y = WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2
ball_vx, ball_vy = BALL_SPEED_X, -BALL_SPEED_Y
score = 0
game_over = False
restart_button = raylib.Rectangle(WIDTH / 2 - 100, HEIGHT / 2 + 40, 200, 44)


def reset_ball():
    """Put the ball back in the middle, keeping its horizontal direction."""
    global ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx, ball_vy
    ball_x, ball_y = WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2
    ball_vx = BALL_SPEED_X if ball_vx >= 0 else -BALL_SPEED_X
    ball_vy = -BALL_SPEED_Y


while not raylib.WindowShouldClose():
    dt = raylib.GetFrameTime()

    # ---- update ----
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_LEFT):
        paddle_x -= PADDLE_SPEED * dt
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_RIGHT):
        paddle_x += PADDLE_SPEED * dt
    paddle_x = max(0.0, min(WIDTH - PADDLE_W, paddle_x))

    if not game_over:
        ball_x += ball_vx * dt
        ball_y += ball_vy * dt

        if ball_x - BALL_R <= 0 and ball_vx < 0:
            ball_x, ball_vx = BALL_R, -ball_vx
        if ball_x + BALL_R >= WIDTH and ball_vx > 0:
            ball_x, ball_vx = WIDTH - BALL_R, -ball_vx
        if ball_y - BALL_R <= 0 and ball_vy < 0:
            ball_y, ball_vy = BALL_R, -ball_vy

        if ball_y + BALL_R >= HEIGHT - PADDLE_H and ball_vy > 0:
            if paddle_x <= ball_x <= paddle_x + PADDLE_W:
                ball_y = HEIGHT - PADDLE_H - BALL_R
                ball_vy = -ball_vy
                score += 1
            else:
                game_over = True
                gcl.set_state("score", score)

    # ---- draw ----
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(int(paddle_x), HEIGHT - PADDLE_H, PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H, raylib.SKYBLUE)
    raylib.DrawCircle(int(ball_x), int(ball_y), BALL_R, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawText(f"score {score}", 20, 20, 30, raylib.RAYWHITE)

    if game_over:
        raylib.DrawText("game over", WIDTH / 2 - 80, HEIGHT / 2 - 40, 30, raylib.RAYWHITE)
        if raygui.GuiButton(restart_button, "Restart"):
            score = 0
            game_over = False
            reset_ball()

    raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: The file runs unchanged whether you launch it with gcl -pyrun keepup.py or let a GCL program start it through Embed.Run(type="python").

sections.title: Where the Pieces Came From
paragraphs: Nothing in this file is new. Each line is a chapter from this track, and recognising that is the point of the project.

sections.title: Sharing the Score With GCL
paragraphs: The one line worth its own note is gcl.set_state("score", score). It publishes the final score into the shared state block, where the GCL program that started this script can read it back with Embed.GetValue(type="python", name="score") after Embed.Stop(type="python") returns.
That is the whole cross-language contract: names, numbers, and a call on each side.
